Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing StreetBrexitDetails of two treaties at heart of Andy Burnham’s EU reset to be publishedGovernment also to publish bill that will enact EU deals, as Tories and Reform hit out over 10-year termination clause

Prefer the Guardian on GoogleDetails of two treaties at the heart of Andy Burnham’s post-Brexit reset plans will be published on Thursday alongside the bill that will implement the changes into UK law.

The treaties signed by the UK and the European Union at last week’s summit will have a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party were to end the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, the BBC reported on Thursday.

Any termination clause could bring the longer-term future of the deal into doubt, after the opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, described it as a “terrible deal” that she would scrap. Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay, with the Reform UK leader promising to renege on the deal if he were to win power, arguing that Burnham “cannot bind a future British government”.

At a major summit in Brussels last week the UK and EU announced three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK.

But uncertainty around the trio of deals remains with fears they could be derailed in six months unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.

On Wednesday Burnham indicated that European students would have to pay higher fees than their domestic equivalents at UK universities.

While Burnham has previously stated he would like to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime, he has played down the issue of full integration since the deal was struck, saying it was “not a prelude to anything” and that it would be “unthinkable” for the UK to rejoin the EU without holding another referendum.

Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food and emissions trading deals, alongside the government’s bill to enact the agreement. The government is also expected to publish assessments of the impact on different sectors and regions of the country .

Earlier this year, the Guardian revealed ministers were planning to reshape Britain’s relationship with the EU with legislation that would result in the UK signing up to EU single market rules without a normal parliamentary vote.

The new bill that will bring into force the food and drink trade deal will contain powers enabling the government to dynamically align with Europe on areas where it has already made agreements. It will also allow the UK to quickly implement evolving single market rules if it determines it is in the national interest, without having to face full parliamentary scrutiny each time.

The European affairs minister, Hamish Falconer, said: “The cutting costs bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements. It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier.”
